title: Nerve Conduction–Electrocardiograms
lead: The currents of this chapter have so far been electrons moving along a wire. In a nerve or a muscle the carriers are sodium, potassium and chlorine ions, and they move across a membrane rather than along a conductor. This section shows how the concentrations on either side of a semipermeable membrane set up a voltage across it, how a stimulus turns that voltage into the pulse called an action potential, how the pulse travels the length of an axon, and how the same process in the heart writes the trace of an electrocardiogram.
objectives: Explain the process by which electric signals are transmitted along a neuron.
Explain the effects myelin sheaths have on signal propagation.
Explain what the features of an ECG signal indicate.
summary_html:
• Electric potentials in neurons and other cells are created by ionic concentration differences across semipermeable membranes.
  • Stimuli change the permeability and create action potentials that propagate along neurons.
  • Myelin sheaths speed this process and reduce the needed energy input.
  • This process in the heart can be measured with an electrocardiogram (ECG).

figures.original_caption: A neuron with its dendrites and long axon. Signals in the form of electric currents reach the cell body through dendrites and across synapses, stimulating the neuron to generate its own signal sent down the axon. The number of interconnections can be far greater than shown here.

The semipermeable membrane of a cell has different concentrations of ions inside and out. Diffusion moves the K+ and Cl− ions in the direction shown, until the Coulomb force halts further transfer. This results in a layer of positive charge on the outside, a layer of negative charge on the inside, and thus a voltage across the cell membrane. The membrane is normally impermeable to Na+.

An action potential is the pulse of voltage inside a nerve cell graphed here. It is caused by movements of ions across the cell membrane as shown. Depolarization occurs when a stimulus makes the membrane permeable to Na+ ions. Repolarization follows as the membrane again becomes impermeable to Na+, and K+ moves from high to low concentration. In the long term, active transport slowly maintains the concentration differences, but the cell may fire hundreds of times in rapid succession without seriously depleting them.

A nerve impulse is the propagation of an action potential along a cell membrane. A stimulus causes an action potential at one location, which changes the permeability of the adjacent membrane, causing an action potential there. This in turn affects the membrane further down, so that the action potential moves slowly (in electrical terms) along the cell membrane. Although the impulse is due to Na+ and K+ going across the membrane, it is equivalent to a wave of charge moving along the outside and inside of the membrane.

The outer surface of the heart changes from positive to negative during depolarization. This wave of depolarization is spreading from the top of the heart and is represented by a vector pointing in the direction of the wave. This vector is a voltage (potential difference) vector. Three electrodes, labeled RA, LA, and LL, are placed on the patient. Each pair (called leads I, II, and III) measures a component of the depolarization vector and is graphed in an ECG.
In a 12-lead ECG, six electrodes are placed on the chest, and four electrodes are placed on the limbs.

exercises.prompt: Note that in Figure 20.25, both the concentration gradient and the Coulomb force tend to move ${\text{Na}}^{+}$ ions into the cell. What prevents this?

answer.solution: The membrane itself prevents it. In its resting state the cell membrane is semipermeable: it lets potassium and chlorine ions through but not sodium ions, so however strongly diffusion and the Coulomb force pull the sodium inward, there is no path for it to take. Both of those influences are real, and they are exactly what makes the stimulated membrane of the next passage behave as it does. The moment a stimulus changes the permeability and opens the membrane to sodium, the ions rush in under both influences at once, and that inrush is the beginning of the action potential.

exercises.prompt: Define depolarization, repolarization, and the action potential.

answer.solution: Depolarization is the loss of the separation of charge across a patch of cell membrane. A stimulus makes the membrane permeable to sodium, the sodium ions rush in, and the inside of the membrane, which was about −90 mV, is first neutralized and then made slightly positive. Repolarization is the return of that separation of charge. The depolarization closes the membrane to sodium again, potassium moves from the high concentration inside to the low concentration outside, and the inside of the membrane falls back to its resting potential. The action potential is the voltage pulse the two of them make together: one rise from the resting potential to a positive peak and one fall back, over a few milliseconds, at one location on the membrane.

exercises.prompt: Explain the properties of myelinated nerves in terms of the insulating properties of myelin.

answer.solution: Myelin is a fatty insulator, and each property of a myelinated axon follows from that. Because an insulator does not let charge pass through it, a signal in one axon cannot leak into the axon beside it, so cross talk is prevented. Because the sheathed stretches carry the signal the way an ordinary conductor with a resistance would, rather than by firing an action potential patch by patch, the signal travels through them very fast and uses no cell energy. What the sheath costs is voltage: there is an $\text{IR}$ signal loss along it, so the pulse arrives at the far end smaller than it began. The unmyelinated gaps, the nodes of Ranvier, make that loss harmless, because in them the pulse triggers a full action potential and is regenerated at full voltage. A myelinated axon is therefore faster, cheaper in energy and better protected than a bare one, and destroying the sheaths, as multiple sclerosis does, takes all three advantages away.

exercises.prompt: Use the ECG in Figure 20.31 to determine the heart rate in beats per minute assuming a constant time between beats.

answer.hint: Read the time from one R peak to the next off the horizontal axis; the rate is the number of such intervals in a minute.

exercises.prompt: A copper wire of length 1.25 m is in a circuit. A current of 2.50 A flows through the wire. (a) Initially, the circuit is at $20.0\text{°}\text{C}$. If there is an energy loss of 3.25 MJ in the first second caused by the wire as soon as the circuit is turned on, what is the radius of the wire? (b) After the wire heats $3.000\text{°}\text{C}$, how much energy is being dissipated by the circuit per second? Neglect the effects of thermal expansion since the wire is considered to be physically constrained from expanding. Assume the current is maintained. (c) At what temperature will the energy dissipation be 1.00% higher than it was at the beginning of the experiment?

parts.hint: The power dissipated is $I^2R$ and the resistance of the wire is $\rho L/A$ with $A = \pi r^2$.
A rise in temperature raises the resistivity through $\rho = \rho_0(1 + \alpha \Delta T)$, and the power follows it.
The dissipation is proportional to the resistivity, so ask what temperature change raises the resistivity by one per cent.

answer.solution:
(a) $\begin{array}{l}\frac{3.25\times {10}^{-3}}{1}\text{j/s}=Power={I}^{2}R=\frac{1}{{r}^{2}}\frac{{(2.50)}^{2}(1.72\times {10}^{-8})(1.25)}{\pi}{\text{jm}}^{2}\text{/s} \\ r=\sqrt{\frac{{(2.50)}^{2}(1.72\times {10}^{-8})(1.25)}{0.00325\pi}}=3.63\text{mm}\end{array}$

(b) $Power=\frac{{(2.50)}^{2}(1.74\times {10}^{-8})(1.25)}{{(3.63\times {10}^{-3})}^{2}\pi}\text{j/s}$, so 3.28 j of energy is expended in 1 s. Since $\alpha$ is specified in the chart to only two significant figures, round to 3.3 j.

(c) Since the energy dissipation is directly proportional to the resistivity, the increase of 0.01% in energy dissipation is when the resistivity increases 1%. Or, $1.01=1+0.0039\Delta T$. $T=23{}^{\circ}\text{C}$.
